Class teacher's note, Class 5 picnic to the botanical park
On the bus this morning I noticed Binita holding a large steel bottle on her lap, nearly twice the size of the others. When I asked, she said, "Last year at the picnic my little bottle finished before lunch, and I was thirsty the whole afternoon. So this year I brought the big one." She had also told her friend Mahima to bring a bigger bottle, and Mahima had. By two o'clock, several children had empty bottles and were asking me for water. Binita and Mahima still had some left, and Binita shared a little with a boy who had none. I have added "one large water bottle" to next year's picnic notice.
- Class teacher

So yesterday I asked Mummy for Papa's big blue bottle, the one he takes to work. It was heavy, but I put it in the side pocket. I also rang Yamini and told her, "Bring your biggest bottle, it gets really hot." She did. At lunch we sat under a tree and I still had half left. Yamini said, "You were right, Vasudha." I felt so clever. Next year I'm also bringing a cap, because my nose is red.

subtype: Approach: staying put and waiting to be found [Thinking]
passage: The school's Diwali mela filled the whole playground with stalls, lights and music. Madhuri was looking at glass bangles at a stall near the stage when she turned round and her mother, Seema, was gone. Her heart jumped into her throat. She wanted to run. Then she remembered what they'd said at home: if you get lost, stop. "Mummy was right here," she thought. "When she notices, she'll come back the way we walked. If I go looking, we'll pass each other." She stood by the bangle stall, next to the lady selling them, and watched the path. Four minutes later Seema came pushing back through the crowd, white-faced. She hugged Madhuri hard. "You stayed where I lost you. That was exactly right."

subtype: Approach: staying put and waiting to be found [Thinking]
passage: I'm Vishal, and I was at the Ganesh festival market with my father when I saw my classmate Shreya standing very still next to the flower stall. Her face was red, like she was about to cry, but she wasn't moving at all. People kept pushing past her. I told my father, "That's Shreya from my class. I think she's lost." Papa went up and asked, gently, "Are you with someone?" She said, "I lost Mummy here. She'll come back this way, so I'm waiting." Papa said, "Good plan. We'll wait with you." We didn't have to wait long. Her mother came rushing back down the same lane, calling her name. I don't know how scared Shreya was inside, but she never took one step away.

Don't wander. Find someone who belongs there. He looked past the people carrying bags and saw an old woman behind a cheese stall with a painted sign, clearly her own shop. He went straight to her. "Excuse me. I'm lost. My name is Pablo Ruiz. My mother is Ana Ruiz. Her number is..." He said it slowly, twice. The woman, whose name tag said Ulla, called the number on her phone. Two minutes later his mother was running between the stalls toward them.

My name is Jeevan Nair. My father is Mohan Nair. His number is..." He said it clearly and slowly. Charu repeated it back. subtype: Approach: following the first friendly adult who offers to help [Pitfall]
passage: At the busy market in Accra, Rafael lost his mother's hand near the fabric stalls. He spun round, crying. A man in a cap bent down. "Looking for your mother? I saw her. Come, she went that way." Rafael didn't stop to think. He followed. They went down one lane, then another. The stalls changed; the noise got quieter. Nothing looked familiar. "She's not here," Rafael said, stopping. The man said, "Just a bit further." A stall-keeper named Kofi, who had seen them pass twice, stepped out. "Boy, who is this man to you?" "Nobody," said Rafael. The man walked off quickly. Kofi called Rafael's mother from the number in Rafael's pocket and stayed with him until she came, twenty minutes later, from the far side of the market. That evening she and Rafael talked about who is safe to ask.

qa.a: Kofi notices something odd about a crying boy passing twice with a man and steps in to protect him.

subtype: Approach: mental rehearsal of a lost-child plan made beforehand [Thinking]

Note in the family diary, Saturday
Before we went into Chandni Chowk today, I stopped with Harsha near the metro exit and asked him, "If we get separated, what will you do?" He thought and said, "Cry?" We laughed, and then made a plan together. He said it aloud three times: "Stop. Find a shop with a counter, not a person walking. Tell them Papa's number. Don't leave the area." He practised Papa's number too. We didn't get separated, thankfully. But on the way home he said it all again without being asked, and told his little cousin the plan as well. I will ask him again before every crowded outing, so the plan stays fresh.
- Sudha

The shopkeeper had it announced, and his mother came.

Round and round the fair, all of us running, never meeting. A policeman finally caught him by the arm and asked where he lived. Gopu knew our address by heart. He had recited it that very morning. But he just cried and couldn't say it. It was an hour before they announced his name and we came. Your great-grandmother didn't let go of him for a week.
